{{Short description|Kind of complex manifold}}
[[Image:Lattice torsion points.svg|right|thumb|300px|The complex torus associated to a lattice spanned by two periods, ω<sub>1</sub> and ω<sub>2</sub>. Corresponding edges are identified.]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''complex torus''' is a particular kind of [[complex manifold]] ''M'' whose underlying [[smooth manifold]] is a [[torus]] in the usual sense (i.e. the [[cartesian product]] of some number ''N'' [[circle]]s). Here ''N'' must be the even number 2''n'', where ''n'' is the [[complex dimension]] of ''M''.

All such complex structures can be obtained as follows: take a [[lattice (group)|lattice]] Λ in a vector space ''V'' isomorphic to '''C'''<sup>''n''</sup> considered as real vector space; then the [[quotient group]]
<math display="block">V/\Lambda</math>
is a [[compact space|compact]] complex manifold. All complex tori, up to isomorphism, are obtained in this way. For ''n'' = 1 this is the classical [[period lattice]] construction of [[elliptic curve]]s. For ''n'' > 1 [[Bernhard Riemann]] found necessary and sufficient conditions for a complex torus to be an [[algebraic variety]]; those that are varieties can be embedded into [[complex projective space]], and are the [[abelian varieties]].

The actual projective embeddings are complicated (see [[equations defining abelian varieties]]) when ''n'' > 1, and are really coextensive with the theory of [[theta-function]]s of [[several complex variable]]s (with fixed modulus). There is nothing as simple as the [[cubic curve]] description for ''n'' = 1. [[Computer algebra]] can handle cases for small ''n'' reasonably well. By [[Algebraic geometry and analytic geometry#Chow.27s theorem|Chow's theorem]], no complex torus other than the abelian varieties can 'fit' into [[projective space]].

== Definition ==
One way to define complex tori<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Mumford|first=David|title=Abelian varieties|date=2008|publisher=Published for the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research|others=C. P. Ramanujam, I︠U︡. I. Manin|isbn=978-8185931869|oclc=297809496}}</ref> is as a compact connected [[complex Lie group|complex]] [[Lie group]] <math>G</math>. These are Lie groups where the structure maps are holomorphic maps of complex manifolds. It turns out that all such compact connected Lie groups are commutative, and are isomorphic to a quotient of their [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g} = T_0G</math> whose covering map is the [[Exponential map (Lie theory)|exponential map]] of a Lie algebra to its associated Lie group. The kernel of this map is a lattice <math>\Lambda \subset \mathfrak{g}</math> and <math>\mathfrak{g}/\Lambda \cong G </math>.

Conversely, given a complex vector space <math>V</math> and a lattice <math>\Lambda \subseteq V</math> of maximal rank, the quotient complex manifold <math>V/\Lambda</math> has a complex Lie group structure, and is also compact and connected. This implies that the two definitions for complex tori are equivalent.

== Period matrix of a complex torus ==
One way to describe a ''g''-dimensional complex torus<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Birkenhake|first=Christina|title=Complex Abelian Varieties|date=2004|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|others=Herbert Lange|isbn=978-3-662-06307-1|edition=Second, augmented|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|oclc=851380558}}</ref>{{rp|9}}  is by using a <math>g\times 2g</math> matrix <math>\Pi</math> whose columns correspond to a basis <math>\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_{2g}</math> of the lattice <math>\Lambda</math> expanded out using a basis <math>e_1,\ldots,e_g</math> of <math>V</math>. That is, we write
<math display="block">\Pi = \begin{pmatrix}
\lambda_{1,1} & \cdots & \lambda_{1,2g} \\
\vdots & & \vdots \\
\lambda_{g,1} & \cdots & \lambda_{g,2g}
\end{pmatrix}</math>
so
<math display="block">\lambda_i = \sum_{j}\lambda_{ji}e_j</math>
We can then write the torus <math>X = V/\Lambda</math> as
<math display="block">X = \mathbb{C}^g/\Pi\mathbb{Z}^{2g}.</math>
If we go in the reverse direction by selecting a matrix <math>\Pi \in Mat_\mathbb{C}(g,2g)</math>, it corresponds to a period matrix if and only if the corresponding matrix <math>P \in Mat_\mathbb{C}(2g,2g)</math> constructed by adjoining the complex conjugate matrix <math>\overline{\Pi}</math> to <math>\Pi</math>, so
<math display="block">P = \begin{pmatrix}
\Pi \\
\overline{\Pi}
\end{pmatrix}</math>
is [[Algebraic curve#Singularities|nonsingular]]. This guarantees the column vectors of <math>\Pi</math> span a lattice in <math>\mathbb{C}^g</math> hence must be linearly independent vectors over <math>\mathbb{R}</math>.

=== Example ===
For a two-dimensional complex torus, it has a period matrix of the form
<math display="block">\Pi = \begin{pmatrix}
\lambda_{1,1} & \lambda_{1,2} & \lambda_{1,3} & \lambda_{1,4} \\
\lambda_{2,1} & \lambda_{2,2} & \lambda_{2,3} & \lambda_{2,4}
\end{pmatrix}</math>
for example, the matrix
<math display="block">\Pi = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & i & 2i \\
1 & -i & 1 & 1
\end{pmatrix}</math>
forms a period matrix since the associated period matrix has determinant 4.

=== Normalized period matrix ===
For any complex torus <math>X = V/\Lambda</math> of dimension <math>g</math> it has a period matrix <math>\Pi</math> of the form
<math display="block">(Z, 1_g)</math>where <math>1_g</math> is the [[identity matrix]] and <math>Z \in Mat_\mathbb{C}(g)</math> where <math>\det\text{Im}(Z) \neq 0</math>. We can get this from taking a [[change of basis]] of the vector space <math>V</math> giving a [[block matrix]] of the form above. The condition for <math>\det\text{Im}(Z) \neq 0</math> follows from looking at the corresponding <math>P</math>-matrix
<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix}
Z & 1_g \\
\overline{Z} & 1_g
\end{pmatrix}</math>
since this must be a non-singular matrix. This is because if we calculate the determinant of the block matrix, this is simply
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\det P &= \det(1_g)\det(Z - 1_g1_g\overline{Z}) \\
&= \det(Z-\overline{Z}) \\
&\Rightarrow \det(\text{Im}(Z)) \neq 0
\end{align}</math>
which gives the implication.

==== Example ====
For example, we can write a normalized period matrix for a 2-dimensional complex torus as
<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix}
z_{1,1} & z_{1,2} & 1 & 0\\
z_{2,1} & z_{2,2} & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}</math>
one such example is the normalized period matrix
<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix}
1+i & 1 - i & 1 & 0\\
1+2i & 1+\sqrt{2}i & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}</math>
since the determinant of <math>\text{Im}(Z)</math> is nonzero, equal to <math>2 + \sqrt{2}</math>.

=== Period matrices of Abelian varieties ===
To get a period matrix which gives a projective complex manifold, hence an algebraic variety, the period matrix needs to further satisfy the [[Riemann bilinear relations]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Riemann bilinear relations|url=https://www2.math.upenn.edu/~chai/papers_pdf/bilinear_relations.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210531181635/https://www2.math.upenn.edu/~chai/papers_pdf/bilinear_relations.pdf|archive-date=31 May 2021}}</ref>

== Homomorphisms of complex tori ==
If we have complex tori <math>X = V/\Lambda</math> and <math>X' = V'/\Lambda'</math> of dimensions <math>g,g'</math>, then a homomorphism<ref name=":0" />{{rp|11}}  of complex tori is a function
<math display="block">f:X \to X'</math>
such that the group structure is preserved. This has a number of consequences, such as every homomorphism induces a map of their covering spaces
<math display="block">F:V \to V'</math>
which is compatible with their covering maps. Furthermore, because <math>F</math> induces a [[group homomorphism]], it must restrict to a morphism of the lattices
<math display="block">F_\Lambda:\Lambda \to \Lambda '</math>In particular, there are injections
<math display="block">\rho_a:\text{Hom}(X,X') \to \text{Hom}_\mathbb{C}(V,V')</math> and <math>\rho_r:\text{Hom}(X,X') \to \text{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(\Lambda,\Lambda')</math>
which are called the analytic and rational representations of the space of homomorphisms. These are useful to determining some information about the endomorphism ring <math>\text{End}(X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}</math> which has rational dimension <math>m \leq 4gg'</math>.

=== Holomorphic maps of complex tori ===
The class of homomorphic maps between complex tori have a very simple structure. Of course, every homomorphism induces a holomorphic map, but every holomorphic map is the composition of a special kind of holomorphic map with a homomorphism. For an element <math>x_0 \in X</math> we define the translation map
<math display="block">t_{x_0}:X\to X</math> sending <math>x \mapsto x+x_0</math> Then, if <math>h</math> is a holomorphic map between complex tori <math>X,X'</math>, there is a unique homomorphism <math>f:X \to X'</math> such that
<math display="block">h = t_{h(0)}\circ f</math>
showing the holomorphic maps are not much larger than the set of homomorphisms of complex tori.

=== Isogenies ===
One distinct class of homomorphisms of complex tori are called isogenies. These are endomorphisms of complex tori with a non-zero kernel. For example, if we let <math>n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\neq 0}</math> be an integer, then there is an associated map
<math display="block">n_X :X\to X</math> sending <math>x\mapsto nx</math> which has kernel
<math display="block">X_n \cong (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{2g}</math>
isomorphic to <math>\Lambda / n\Lambda</math>.

=== Isomorphic complex tori ===
There is an isomorphism of complex structures on the real vector space <math>\mathbb{R}^{2g}</math> and the set
<math display="block">GL_\mathbb{R}(2g)/GL_\mathbb{C}(g)</math>
and isomorphic tori can be given by a change of basis of their lattices, hence a matrix in <math>GL_\mathbb{Z}(2g)</math>. This gives the set of isomorphism classes of complex tori of dimension <math>g</math>, <math>\mathcal{T}_g</math>, as the Double coset space
<math display="block">\mathcal{T}_g \cong GL_\mathbb{Z}(2g)\backslash GL_\mathbb{R}(2g)
/GL_\mathbb{C}(g)</math>
Note that as a real manifold, this has dimension
<math display="block">4g^2 - 2g^2 = 2g^2</math>
this is important when considering the dimensions of [[Moduli of abelian varieties|moduli of Abelian varieties]], which shows that there are far more complex tori than Abelian varieties.

== Line bundles and automorphic forms ==
For complex manifolds <math>X</math>, in particular complex tori, there is a construction<ref name=":0" />{{rp|571}} relating the holomorphic [[line bundle]]s <math>L \to X</math> whose pullback <math>\pi^*L \to \tilde{X}</math> are trivial using the [[group cohomology]] of <math>\pi_1(X)</math>. Fortunately for complex tori, every complex line bundle <math>\pi^*L</math> becomes trivial since <math>\tilde{X} \cong \mathbb{C}^n</math>.

=== Factors of automorphy ===
Starting from the first group cohomology group
<math display="block">H^1(\pi_1(X),H^0(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{X}}^*))</math>we recall how its elements can be represented. Since <math>\pi_1(X)</math> acts on <math>\tilde{X}</math> there is an induced action on all of its sheaves, hence on
<math display="block">H^0(\mathcal{O}^*_{\tilde{X}}) = \{ f: \tilde{X} \to \mathbb{C}^* \}</math>The <math>\pi_1(X)</math>-action can then be represented as a holomorphic map <math>f:\pi_1(X)\times\tilde{X} \to \mathbb{C}^*</math>. This map satisfies the cocycle condition if
<math display="block">f(a\cdot b, x) = f(a,b\cdot x)f(b, x)</math>
for every <math>a,b \in \pi_1(X)</math> and <math>x \in \tilde{X}</math>. The [[abelian group]] of 1-cocycles <math>Z^1(\pi_1(X),H^0(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde{X}}^*))</math> is called the group of '''factors of automorphy'''. Note that such functions <math>f</math> are also just called '''factors'''.

==== On complex tori ====
For complex tori, these functions <math>f</math> are given by functions
<math display="block">f:\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{Z}^{2n} \to \mathbb{C}^*</math>
which follow the cocycle condition. These are [[automorphic function]]s, more precisely, the automorphic functions used in the transformation laws for [[Theta function of a lattice|theta functions]]. Also, any such map can be written as
<math display="block">f = \exp(2 \pi i \cdot g)</math>
for
<math display="block">g:V\times\Lambda \to \mathbb{C}</math>
which is useful for computing invariants related to the associated line bundle.

=== Line bundles from factors of automorphy ===
Given a factor of automorphy <math>f</math> we can define a line bundle on <math>X</math> as follows: the trivial line bundle <math>\tilde{X}\times\mathbb{C} \to \tilde{X}</math> has a <math>\pi_1(X)</math>-action given by
<math display="block">a\cdot (x,t) = (a\cdot x, f(a,x)\cdot t)</math>
for the factor <math>f</math>. Since this action is free and properly discontinuous, the quotient bundle
<math display="block">L = \tilde{X}\times \mathbb{C}/\pi_1(X)</math>
is a complex manifold. Furthermore, the projection <math>p:L \to X</math> induced from the covering projection <math>\pi:\tilde{X}\to X</math>. This gives a map
<math display="block">Z^1(\pi_1(X),H^0(\mathcal{O}_\tilde{X}^*)) \to H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X^*)</math>
which induces an isomorphism
<math display="block">H^1(\pi_1(X),H^0(\mathcal{O}_\tilde{X}^*)) \to \ker(H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X^*) \to H^1(\tilde{X},\mathcal{O}_\tilde{X}^*))</math>
giving the desired result.

==== For complex tori ====
In the case of complex tori, we have <math>H^1(\tilde{X},\mathcal{O}_\tilde{X}^*)\cong 0</math> hence there is an isomorphism
<math display="block">H^1(\pi_1(X),H^0(\mathcal{O}_\tilde{X}^*)) \cong H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X^*)</math>
representing line bundles on complex tori as 1-cocyles in the associated group cohomology. It is typical to write down the group <math>\pi_1(X)</math> as the lattice <math>\Lambda</math> defining <math>X</math>, hence
<math display="block">H^1(\Lambda,H^0(\mathcal{O}_V^*))</math>
contains the isomorphism classes of line bundles on <math>X</math>.

==== First chern class of line bundles on complex tori ====
From the [[Exponential sheaf sequence|exponential exact sequence]]
<math display="block">0 \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathcal{O}_X \to \mathcal{O}_X^* \to 0</math>the connecting morphism
<math display="block">c_1:H^1(\mathcal{O}_X^*) \to H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})</math>
is the first [[Chern class]] map, sending an isomorphism class of a line bundle to its associated first Chern class. It turns out that there is an isomorphism between <math>H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})</math> and the module of alternating forms on the lattice <math>\Lambda</math>, <math>Alt^2(\Lambda, \mathbb{Z})</math>. Therefore, <math>c_1(L)</math> can be considered as an alternating <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-valued 2-form <math>E_L</math> on <math>\Lambda</math>. If <math>L</math> has factor of automorphy <math>f = \exp(2\pi i g)</math> then the alternating form can be expressed as
<math display="block">E_L(\lambda, \mu) = g(\mu, v+\lambda) + g(\lambda, v) - g(\lambda, v + \mu) - g(\mu, v)</math>for <math>\mu,\lambda \in \Lambda</math> and <math>v \in V</math>.

===== Example =====
For a normalized period matrix
<math display="block">\Pi = \begin{pmatrix}
z_{1,1} & z_{1,2} & 1 & 0 \\
z_{2,1} & z_{2,2} & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}</math>
expanded using the standard basis of <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math> we have the column vectors defining the lattice <math>\Lambda \subset \mathbb{C}^2</math>. Then, any alternating form <math>E_L</math> on <math>\Lambda</math> is of the form
<math display="block">E_L = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & e_{2,1} & e_{3,1} & e_{4,1} \\
-e_{2,1} & 0 & e_{3,2} & e_{4,2} \\
-e_{3,1} & -e_{3,2} & 0 & e_{4,3} \\ 
-e_{4,1} & -e_{4,2} & -e_{4,3} & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>
where a number of compatibility conditions must be satisfied.

=== Sections of line bundles and theta functions ===
For a line bundle <math>L</math> given by a factor of automorphy <math>f:\Lambda\times V \to \mathbb{C}^{*}</math>, so <math>[f] \in H^1(\Lambda, H^0(V,\mathcal{O}_V^*))</math> and <math>\phi_1[f] = [L] \in \text{Pic}(X)</math>, there is an associated sheaf of sections <math>\mathcal{L}</math> where
<math display="block">\mathcal{L}(U) = \left\{
\theta:\pi^{-1}(U) \to \mathbb{C} : \begin{matrix}
\theta \text{ holomorphic with } \theta(v+\lambda) = f(\lambda,v)\theta(v) \\
\text{for all } (\lambda, v) \in \Lambda \times \pi^{-1}(U)
\end{matrix}
\right\}</math>
with <math>U \subset X</math> open. Then, evaluated on global sections, this is the set of holomorphic functions <math>\theta: V \to \mathbb{C}</math> such that
<math display="block">\theta(v + \lambda) = f(\lambda, v)\theta(v)</math>
which are exactly the theta functions on the plane. Conversely, this process can be done backwards where the automorphic factor in the theta function is in fact the factor of automorphy defining a line bundle on a complex torus.

== Hermitian forms and the Appell-Humbert theorem ==
{{See also|Appell–Humbert theorem}}
For the alternating <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-valued 2-form <math>E_L</math> associated to the line bundle <math>L \to X</math>, it can be extended to be <math>\mathbb{R}</math>-valued. Then, it turns out that any <math>\mathbb{R}</math>-valued alternating form <math>E:V\times V \to \mathbb{R}</math> satisfying the following conditions

# <math>E(\Lambda,\Lambda)\subseteq \mathbb{Z}</math>
# <math>E(iv,iw) = E(v,w)</math> for any <math>v,w\in V</math>

is the extension of some first Chern class <math>c_1(L)</math> of a line bundle <math>L \to X</math>. Moreover, there is an associated Hermitian form <math>H:V\times V \to \mathbb{C}</math> satisfying

# <math>\text{Im}H(v,w) = E(v,w)</math>
# <math>H(v,w) = E(iv,w) + iE(v,w)</math>

for any <math>v,w \in V</math>.

=== Néron-Severi group ===
{{See also|Néron–Severi group}}
For a complex torus <math>X = V/\Lambda</math> we can define the '''Néron-Serveri group''' <math>NS(X)</math> as the group of Hermitian forms <math>H</math> on <math>V</math> with
<math display="block">\text{Im}H(\Lambda,\Lambda) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}</math>
Equivalently, it is the image of the homomorphism
<math display="block">c_1:H^1(\mathcal{O}_X^*) \to H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})</math>
from the first Chern class. We can also identify it with the group of real-valued alternating forms <math>E</math> on <math>V</math> such that <math>E(\Lambda,\Lambda)\subseteq \mathbb{Z}</math>.

=== Example of a Hermitian form on an elliptic curve ===
For<ref>{{Cite web|title=How Appell-Humbert theorem works in the simplest case of an elliptic curve|url=https://math.stackexchange.com/a/1113513}}</ref> an elliptic curve <math>\mathcal{E}</math> given by the lattice <math>\begin{pmatrix}1 & \tau \end{pmatrix}</math> where <math>\tau \in \mathbb{H}</math> we can find the integral form <math>E \in \text{Alt}^2(\Lambda,\mathbb{Z})</math> by looking at a generic alternating matrix and finding the correct compatibility conditions for it to behave as expected. If we use the standard basis <math>x_1,y_1</math> of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>
as a real vector space (so <math>z = z_1 + iz_2 = z_1x_1 + z_2y_1 </math>), then we can write out an alternating matrix
<math display="block">E = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & e \\
-e & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>
and calculate the associated products on the vectors associated to <math>1,\tau</math>. These are
<math display="block">\begin{align}
E\cdot \begin{pmatrix}
1 \\ 0
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
0 \\ -e
\end{pmatrix} & &
E\cdot \begin{pmatrix}
\tau_1 \\ \tau_2
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
e\tau_2 \\ -e\tau_1
\end{pmatrix}
\end{align}</math>
Then, taking the inner products (with the standard inner product) of these vectors with the vectors <math>1,\tau</math> we get
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\ 0
\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}
0 \\ -e
\end{pmatrix} = 0
&&
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_1 \\ \tau_2
\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}
0 \\ -e
\end{pmatrix} = -e\tau_2  \\

\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\ 0
\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}
e\tau_2 \\ -e\tau_1
\end{pmatrix} = e\tau_2

&&
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_1 \\ \tau_2
\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}
e\tau_2 \\ -e\tau_1
\end{pmatrix} = 0
\end{align}</math>
so if <math>E(\Lambda,\Lambda) \subset \mathbb{Z}</math>, then
<math display="block">e = a\frac{1}{\text{Im}(\tau)}</math>
We can then directly verify <math>E(v,w) = E(iv,iw)</math>, which holds for the matrix above. For a fixed <math>a</math>, we will write the integral form as <math>E_a</math>. Then, there is an associated Hermitian form
<math display="block">H_a:\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}</math>
given by
<math display="block">H_a(z,w) = a\cdot \frac{z\overline{w}}{\text{Im}(\tau)}</math>
where <math>a \in \mathbb{Z}</math>

=== Semi-character pairs for Hermitian forms ===
For a Hermitian form <math>H</math> a semi-character is a map
<math>\chi:\Lambda \to U(1)</math>
such that
<math display="block">\chi(\lambda + \mu) = \chi(\lambda)\chi(\mu)\exp(i\pi \text{Im}H(\lambda, \mu))</math>
hence the map <math>\chi</math> behaves like a [[Character (mathematics)|character]] twisted by the Hermitian form. Note that if <math>H</math> is the zero element in <math>NS(X)</math>, so it corresponds to the trivial line bundle <math>\mathbb{C}\times X \to X</math>, then the associated semi-characters are the [[Character group|group of characters]] on <math>\Lambda</math>. It will turn out that this corresponds to the group <math>\text{Pic}^0(X)</math> of degree <math>0</math> line bundles on <math>X</math>, or equivalently, its dual torus, which can be seen by computing the group of characters
<math>\text{Hom}(\Lambda, U(1))</math>
whose elements can be factored as maps
<math>\Lambda \to \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} \cong U(1)</math>
showing a character is of the form
<math>\chi(\cdot) = \exp\left(2\pi i v^*(\cdot) \right)</math>
for some fixed dual lattice vector <math>v^* \in  \Lambda^*</math>. This gives the isomorphism
<math>\text{Hom}(\Lambda, U(1)) \cong \mathbb{R}^{2g}/\mathbb{Z}^{2g}</math>
of the set of characters with a real torus. The set of all pairs of semi-characters and their associated Hermitian form <math>(\chi, H)</math>, or '''semi-character pairs''', forms a group <math>\mathcal{P}(\Lambda)</math> where
<math display="block">(H_1,\chi_1)*(H_2,\chi_2) = (H_1 + H_2,\chi_1\chi_2)</math>
This group structure comes from applying the previous commutation law for semi-characters to the new semicharacter <math>\chi_1\chi_2</math>:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\chi_1\chi_2(\lambda + \mu) &= \chi_1(\lambda+\mu)\chi_2(\lambda+\mu) \\
&= \chi_1(\lambda)\chi_1(\mu)\chi_2(\lambda)\chi_2(\mu)\exp(i\pi\text{Im}H_1(\lambda,\mu))\exp(i\pi\text{Im}H_2(\lambda,\mu)) \\
&= \chi_1\chi_2(\lambda)\chi_1\chi_2(\mu)\exp(
i\pi\text{Im}H_1(\lambda,\mu) + i\pi\text{Im}H_2(\lambda,\mu)
)
\end{align}</math>
It turns out this group surjects onto <math>NS(X)</math> and has kernel <math>\text{Hom}(\Lambda,U(1))</math>, giving a short exact sequence
<math display="block">1 \to \text{Hom}(\Lambda, U(1)) \to \mathcal{P}(\Lambda) \to NS(X) \to 1</math>
This surjection can be constructed through associating to every semi-character pair a line bundle <math>L(H,\chi)</math>.

=== Semi-character pairs and line bundles ===
For a semi-character pair <math>(H,\chi)</math> we can construct a 1-cocycle <math>a_{(H,\chi)}</math> on <math>\Lambda</math> as a map
<math display="block">a_{(H,\chi)}:\Lambda\times V \to \mathbb{C}^*</math>defined as
<math display="block">a(\lambda, v) = \chi(\lambda)\exp(\pi H(v,\lambda) + \frac{\pi}{2} H(\lambda,\lambda))</math>
The cocycle relation
<math display="block">a(\lambda+\mu, v) = a(\lambda, v+\mu)a(\mu,v)</math>
can be easily verified by direct computation. Hence the cocycle determines a line bundle
<math display="block">L(H,\chi) \cong V\times \mathbb{C}/\Lambda</math>
where the <math>\Lambda</math>-action on <math>V\times \mathbb{C}</math> is given by
<math display="block">\lambda\circ(v,t)= (v+t, a_{(H,\chi)}(\lambda, v)t)</math>
Note this action can be used to show the sections of the line bundle <math>L(H,\chi)</math> are given by the theta functions with factor of automorphy <math>a_{(H,\chi)}</math>. Sometimes, this is called the '''canonical factor of automorphy''' for <math>L</math>. Note that because every line bundle <math>L \to X</math> has an associated Hermitian form <math>H</math>, and a semi-character can be constructed using the factor of automorphy for <math>L</math>, we get a surjection
<math display="block">\mathcal{P}(\Lambda) \to \text{Pic}(X)</math>
Moreover, this is a group homomorphism with a trivial kernel. These facts can all be summarized in the following commutative diagram
<math display="block">\begin{matrix}
1 & \to & \text{Hom}(\Lambda, U(1)) & \to &\mathcal{P}(\Lambda) & \to & NS(X) & \to 0 \\
& & \downarrow & & \downarrow & & \downarrow \\
1 & \to & \text{Pic}^0(X) & \to & \text{Pic}(X) & \to & \text{NS}(X) & \to 0
\end{matrix}</math>
where the vertical arrows are isomorphisms, or equality. This diagram is typically called the '''Appell-Humbert theorem'''.

== Dual complex torus ==
{{See also|Poincaré bundle|Dual abelian variety}}

As mentioned before, a character on the lattice can be expressed as a function
<math display="block">\chi(\cdot) = \exp\left(2\pi i v^*(\cdot) \right)</math>
for some fixed dual vector <math>v^*\in\Lambda^*</math>. If we want to put a complex structure on the real torus of all characters, we need to start with a complex vector space which <math>\Lambda^*</math> embeds into. It turns out that the complex vector space
<math display="block">\overline{\Omega} = \text{Hom}_{\overline{\mathbb{C}}}(V,\mathbb{C})</math>
of complex [[Antilinear map|antilinear]] maps, is isomorphic to the real dual vector space <math>\text{Hom}_\mathbb{R}(V,\mathbb{R})</math>, which is part of the factorization for writing down characters. Furthermore, there is an associated lattice
<math display="block">\hat{\Lambda} = \{ l \in \overline{\Omega} : \langle l, \Lambda \rangle \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \}</math>
called the dual lattice of <math>\Lambda</math>. Then, we can form the '''dual complex torus'''
<math display="block">\hat{X} \cong \overline{\Omega}/\hat{\Lambda}</math>
which has the special property that that dual of the dual complex torus is the original complex torus. Moreover, from the discussion above, we can identify the dual complex torus with the Picard group of <math>X</math>
<math display="block">\hat{X} \cong \text{Pic}^0(X)</math>
by sending an anti-linear dual vector <math>l</math> to
<math display="block">l \mapsto \exp(2\pi i \langle l, \cdot \rangle)</math>
giving the map
<math display="block">\overline{\Omega} \to \text{Hom}(\Lambda,U(1))</math>
which factors through the dual complex torus. There are other constructions of the dual complex torus using techniques from the theory of Abelian varieties.<ref name=":1" />{{rp|123–125}} Essentially, taking a line bundle <math>L</math> over a complex torus (or Abelian variety) <math>X</math>, there is a closed subset <math>K(L)</math> of <math>X</math> defined as the points of <math>x\in X</math> where their translations are invariant, i.e.
<math display="block">T^*_x(L) \cong L</math>
Then, the dual complex torus can be constructed as
<math display="block">\hat{X} := X/K(L)</math>
presenting it as an isogeny. It can be shown that defining <math>\hat{X}</math> this way satisfied the universal properties of <math>\text{Pic}^0(X)</math>, hence is in fact the dual complex torus (or Abelian variety).

=== Poincaré bundle ===
From the construction of the dual complex torus, it is suggested that there should exist a line bundle <math>\mathcal{P}</math> over the product of the torus <math>X</math> and its dual which can be used to present all isomorphism classes of degree 0 line bundles on <math>X</math>. We can encode this behavior with the following two properties

# <math>\mathcal{P}|_{X\times \{[L]\}} \cong L</math> for any point <math>[L] \in \hat{X}</math> giving the line bundle <math>L</math>
# <math>\mathcal{P}|_{\{0\}\times \hat{X}}</math> is a trivial line bundle

where the first is the property discussed above, and the second acts as a normalization property. We can construct <math>\mathcal{P}</math> using the following hermitian form
<math display="block">\begin{matrix}
H:(V\times \overline{\Omega})\times(V\times \overline{\Omega}) \to \mathbb{C} \\
H((v_1,l_1),(v_2,l_2)) = \overline{l_2(v_1)} + l_1(v_2)
\end{matrix}</math>
and the semi-character
<math display="block">\begin{matrix}
\chi:\Lambda\times\hat{\Lambda} \to U(1) \\
\chi(\lambda,l_0) = \exp(i\pi \text{Im}l_0(\lambda))
\end{matrix}</math>
for <math>H</math>. Showing this data constructs a line bundle with the desired properties follows from looking at the associated canonical factor of <math>(H,\chi)</math>, and observing its behavior at various restrictions.
